questions.q: A model says the probability a machine fails this month is 0.25. What does that mean?
options: The machine will be broken for a quarter of the month
In the long run, about one month in four like this one would see a failure
The machine will definitely fail within four months
The model is 25% sure it is correct
questions.why: A probability measures how often an event happens in the long run: 0.25 is about one time in four. Reading it as "definitely within four months" turns a chance into a schedule; each month is still uncertain.

questions.q: Roll one fair die. What is P(even number or a number greater than 4)?
questions.why: P(even) = 3/6, P(greater than 4) = 2/6, and the overlap {6} = 1/6. Addition rule: 3/6 + 2/6 − 1/6 = 4/6 = **2/3** (the outcomes 2, 4, 5, 6). 5/6 forgets to subtract the overlap, so 6 is counted twice.

questions.q: 2% of patients have a condition. A test detects 95% of true cases but also flags 10% of healthy patients. A patient tests positive. What is the probability they have the condition?
options: About 95%
About 90%
About 16%
About 2%
questions.why: Imagine 10,000 patients: 200 ill, 190 flagged; 9,800 healthy, 980 flagged. P(ill | positive) = 190 / 1,170 ≈ **16%**. Answering 95% confuses P(positive | ill) with P(ill | positive), the base-rate fallacy; 2% ignores the evidence altogether.

questions.q: Of 1,000 baskets, 500 contain coffee, 200 contain milk and 100 contain both. What does this tell you about coffee and milk?
options: They look independent: P(milk | coffee) = 0.2, the same as P(milk) overall, so the lift is 1
They are strongly associated, because 100 baskets have both
Coffee buyers are half as likely to buy milk
Milk causes people to buy coffee
questions.why: P(milk | coffee) = 100 / 500 = 0.2 and P(milk) = 0.2, so lift = 1.0; equivalently P(both) = 0.1 = 0.5 × 0.2. A large count of joint baskets is the tempting signal, but it is exactly what chance alone predicts here. Association, even when present, would not show causation.

questions.q: A factory has three independent machines, each with a 10% chance of failing this month. What is the probability that at least one fails?
questions.why: Use the complement: P(none fail) = 0.9³ = 0.729, so P(at least one) = 1 − 0.729 = **0.271**. Adding 0.1 three times (0.30) double-counts the months where two machines fail; 0.729 is the chance none fail.

questions.q: Sending a coupon costs ₹50. 25% of customers redeem it and spend an extra ₹400, on which the margin is 30%. What is the expected net value per customer?
questions.why: Expected extra margin = 0.25 × ₹400 × 0.30 = ₹30; minus the ₹50 cost gives **−₹20**. Using spend instead of margin gives 0.25 × 400 − 50 = +₹50, which makes a loss-making campaign look profitable.

questions.q: Two temperature alarms on the same machine each trigger on 5% of days. An engineer estimates P(both) = 0.05 × 0.05 = 0.0025, but the logs show both trigger on 4% of days. How should you read this?
options: The logs must be wrong, because the multiplication rule is exact
Both alarms should be removed because they disagree
The alarms are independent but unreliable
The alarms are not independent: given one triggers, the other does 0.04 / 0.05 = 80% of the time, probably because they respond to the same cause
questions.why: Multiplying probabilities is only valid for independent events. P(B | A) = 0.04 / 0.05 = 0.8, far above 0.05, so knowing one alarm fired changes the chance of the other. Trusting the multiplication over the data is the classic mistake.

questions.q: Interview: "Your fraud model catches 90% of fraud. A stakeholder says that means 90% of flagged transactions are fraud. What do you tell them?" Which answer is best?
options: They are right; the two numbers are the same
That confuses P(flagged | fraud) with P(fraud | flagged); when fraud is rare, most flags can be false alarms, so you need the base rate and the false-alarm rate to work out the second
The second number is always higher than the first
Only the 90% matters for decisions
questions.why: With 1% fraud and 5% of legitimate transactions flagged, only about 15% of flags are fraud even with 90% detection. Swapping the order of a conditional probability is the base-rate fallacy; the share of flags that are genuine (precision) is what the operations team actually experiences.
